To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have observed electron field emission from carbon nanofibres grown in a conventional rf-PECVD reactor at room temperature.
we have shown the possibility of electron emission from room-temperature grown carbon nanofiber at a low macroscopic electric field.
we have demonstrated electron field emission at room temperature from carbon nanofibres grown by a chemical vapour deposition process using methane as a carbon source.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the growth, characterization, and application of nanofibers as electron field emitters.
the growth and field emission properties of carbon nanofibres.
the synthesis and characterization of carbon nanofibres and the study of their field emission properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the field enhancement mechanism for electron emission from carbon nanofibres grown in a conventional plasma enhanced chemical vapour deposition reactor is the same as that from carbon nanotubes grown by chemical vapour deposition.
electron field emission from carbon nanofibres is possible at low macroscopic fields and that the emission is from the nanofibres themselves and not from any surrounding amorphous film.
the field enhancement factor of these carbon nanofibrous emitters are in the range 10–20.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the field emission characteristics of carbon nanotubes and nanofibers grown in a conventional plasma enhanced chemical vapor depositions reactor can be controlled by the growth process.
the field induced emission from carbon nanofibres is due to the presence of sharp tips on the carbon nanofibre.
the field emission properties of the carbon nanofibres are comparable to those of carbon nanotubes, and that the nanotubes are not necessary to achieve field emission from a carbon based material.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the nanofiber emitters have a lower threshold for field emission than other carbon based field emitters and that the emitters are grown directly on the cathode substrate, eliminating the need for a transfer process.
the carbon nanofiber material system is an excellent candidate material for the development of field emission devices.
the nanofiber morphology and the field enhancement at the tip is responsible for the low threshold field of emission.
